report:
(Fictional case study for training. Not a real investigation.)

Executive summary

On 18/06/2026 Saltbush Air SB512, a 50-seat twin-turboprop registered VH-SBQ, rejected its take-off on runway 09 at Tarlton Springs Aerodrome at 118 kt, six knots above a V1 of 112 kt. Times in this report are local time (UTC+10). The aircraft struck two kangaroos at 114 kt, left the end of the runway at approximately 21 kt and stopped 62 m into the 90 m runway end safety area, upright and on the extended centreline. There were 44 passengers, 2 flight crew and 1 cabin crew on board. Nobody was seriously injured, and one cabin crew member reported bruising during the disembarkation. The aircraft sustained substantial damage, including three No. 2 propeller blades beyond limits, damage to the right inboard flap and wing lower surface, distorted right main gear doors and both right main tyres deflated. The aerodrome closed for 4 hours 20 minutes.

The stop ran out of runway because of two contributions, and neither alone reaches the end. The reject began 3 seconds and 6 kt past V1, at 1,152 m, leaving 695 m of sealed surface against a scheduled accelerate-stop distance of 1,780 m and a distance available of 1,847 m. The strike then took the No. 2 propeller out of the stop, so mean deceleration was 2.6 m/s2, approximately 15% below the certified value, and the stop needed 757 m.

The animals reached the runway because of conditions that were known and not acted on. The northern boundary fence had been recorded as failed and left unrepaired through three budget rounds. The departure fell in the period when 38 of the 41 logged kangaroo sightings occurred. No runway inspection was requested, and it is very likely that this followed from Appendix 8A listing an aerodrome only after a reported wildlife strike. The aerodrome operator was not in breach of AS-139, because the threshold for a documented wildlife plan did not apply to it, and it is likely that this left the fence a deferrable works item. The roll began in darkness, five minutes after the end of civil twilight with no moon, and it is likely that this contributed to the late sighting. The evening service had been approved without reopening the daylight-only assessment RRA-041 issue 3, which likely led to that departure after last light. The operator gave crews no training or guidance for an obstruction during the take-off roll, and that likely contributed to the reject above V1.

Maximum braking was established 2 seconds after the decision against a fleet mean of 3.2 seconds, which very likely reduced the risk, and the passengers disembarked without an evacuation. Performance assessment PEA-2026-0417 found that a continued take-off would likely have been worse, so rejecting was likely the safest course available. That does not make the decision compliant with Part B 4.6.4.

Two matters are still being examined, namely the 24-month check interval for floor escape path lighting and the intensity of four northern edge lights. Two further matters, crew fatigue and the effect of the edge lights, could not be settled.

Safety actions so far are:

  • The evening service was suspended on 19/06/2026.
  • Temporary revision TR-2026-04 listed Tarlton Springs on 26/06/2026.
  • Fence item WR-221 was funded and its replacement programmed for 09/2026, with temporary electric wire installed on 25/06/2026.
  • Two recommendations are open, with responses due 30/09/2026. They concern the Appendix 8A listing criterion and guidance and training for a runway obstruction during the take-off roll.

Event overview

Aircraft, crew and flight

On 18/06/2026 Saltbush Air flight SB512, a 50-seat twin-turboprop registered VH-SBQ, was to fly from Tarlton Springs Aerodrome to Port Carrick. It carried 44 passengers, 2 flight crew and 1 cabin crew. The calculated take-off weight was 20,800 kg, with flap 10 on a dry runway 09, and the crew's performance entry used a 5 kt headwind component, giving a V1 of 112 kt.

The pilot in command held 8,410 hours in total, 2,140 of them on type. The first officer held 1,655 hours in total, 405 of them on type, and was the pilot flying. The last simulator check and line check for the pilot in command were satisfactory, as was the last simulator check for the first officer. The first officer had flown two earlier sectors into Tarlton Springs, both in daylight. Both crew were tested for drugs and alcohol after the occurrence and both results were negative.

The crew signed on at 06:30. They flew Port Carrick to Hensby, Hensby to Mardle Creek and Mardle Creek to Port Carrick as rostered. SB511 and SB512 were then added to their duty that morning when a member of the rostered crew reported unfit. SB512 was the fifth sector and the roll began 11 hours 00 minutes into a duty planned at 13 hours 00 minutes, against a maximum permitted duty of 13 hours 30 minutes. The pilot in command's duty and rest in the preceding 7 days were within limits with no variations applied. A ground delay at Port Carrick during the third sector was recovered on the Tarlton Springs turnaround, and the doors were closed at 17:16 for a scheduled off-blocks time of 17:20.

Aerodrome, weather and light

Tarlton Springs has no control tower, so crews make their own broadcasts on the CTAF, and the runway lighting is pilot-activated. Runway 09/27 is its only runway. The route risk assessment for the aerodrome, RRA-041, records no alternate within 200 nm at night.

The aerodrome's automatic weather station reported wind of 080 at 8 kt at 16:00, 090 at 7 kt at 16:30, 090 at 6 kt at 17:00 and 090 at 5 kt at 18:00. Visibility was 9999 and the only cloud was few or scattered at 4,000 ft, with no rain. The crew heard an AWIS of 090 at 6 kt shortly before lining up, and the flight data recorder gave a headwind component of 4 to 6 kt during the roll.

Sunset was at 16:58 and civil twilight ended at 17:25. The moon rose at 22:41 and was 14% illuminated. The roll began at 17:30, 5 minutes after the end of civil twilight and with the moon below the horizon.

Sequence of events

The aerodrome's only runway inspection that day was carried out at 07:35, before the first scheduled arrival, and recorded the movement area as clear. No further inspection was carried out or requested.

At 17:21:50 the crew keyed the pilot-activated runway lighting. The pilot in command remarked, "Lights are on. That's thirty minutes on the timer." The crew taxied for runway 09 after a broadcast at 17:23:15 and broadcast again at 17:29:10 that they were lining up. Neither the CVR nor the CTAF recording contains any request for a runway inspection, any offer of one, or any mention of wildlife before departure. At 17:29:22 the pilot in command said, "nobody else about" and handed the take-off to the first officer.

Power was set at 17:30:02, with torque of 98.4% and 98.5% on the two engines. The recorded data show both engines within 0.1% of each other and no caution or warning until the reject. The 80 kt cross-check was normal, and the pilot in command called "V one" at 17:30:29 at 112 kt.

At 17:30:31 the first officer called "Roos - roos, roos, on the left, they're on the -". The aircraft reached VR, 116 kt, in the same second and no rotate call was made. At 17:30:32 the pilot in command said "Stopping. I have control." The power levers reached flight idle within 0.6 seconds, at 118 kt, 6 kt and 3 seconds past V1. Distance reconstruction from recorded groundspeed put the aircraft 1,152 m along the runway at that point, with 695 m of sealed surface remaining (Figure 5).

At 17:30:33 the aircraft struck both animals at 114 kt. The recorder shows a lateral acceleration spike of 0.31 g to the right and a vertical spike of 1.48 g. The first officer said, "(unintelligible) took one on the prop." Maximum braking was established at 17:30:34, 2 seconds after the decision, with anti-skid active on all four wheels. At 17:30:36 the pilot in command called, "Reverse - number two's not coming. Max brakes, max brakes." Reverse was selected on No. 1 only, and the No. 2 propeller RPM decayed from the moment of impact.

At 17:30:47 the pilot in command said, "We're not stopping on it." The aircraft left the sealed surface at 21 kt at 17:30:51, and the deceleration fell from 2.6 m/s2 on the seal to 1.9 m/s2 in graded gravel. It stopped at 17:30:57, 62 m into the 90 m runway end safety area, upright and on the extended centreline, with the nose wheel in graded gravel. The stopping distance from 118 kt was 757 m. There was no fire.

The crew accounts of the sighting differ in what each recorded. On the CVR at 17:32:35 the first officer said the animals "came out of the dark on the left of the strip, crossed the centreline", and estimated the range at first sight at around 200 m. On the CVR at 17:32:47 the pilot in command said, "I never had them. I was heads-in on the engine page after V one." The pilot in command's air safety report (ASR-2026-1184) says that after the first officer's call the pilot in command looked up and saw two large animals on the sealed surface moving from left to right across the centreline. The report also says the decision to reject was made because continuing would leave the aircraft airborne at night with damage the crew could not assess. The pilot in command also reported having stopped above V1 knowingly.

Aftermath

The pilot in command set the parking brake and shut both engines down at 17:31:26, with no fire indications and nothing on the warning panel, and decided not to evacuate. The cabin was told to remain seated. At 17:31:54 the pilot in command reported the situation to the aerodrome reporting officer on the CTAF and requested the aerodrome emergency plan. The aerodrome reporting officer activated it at 17:32:10, dispatched a vehicle, and at 17:32:24 broadcast that runway 09/27 was obstructed and the aerodrome closed.

Passengers disembarked by the forward airstair, which was operating at 17:34:40, with the main cabin lights on, no evacuation commanded and no slides deployed. The timeline gives the disembarkation as 17:34:40 to 17:38:48, an interval of 4 minutes 8 seconds. The occurrence notification gives 4 minutes 8 seconds after the aircraft stopped. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the 4 minutes 8 seconds is the duration of the disembarkation or the time from the stop to passengers clear] While walking back through the cabin during the disembarkation, the first officer noticed sections of the aisle floor strip unlit.

The aerodrome was closed for 4 hours 20 minutes. VH-SBQ was quarantined at Tarlton Springs and the flight recorders were removed on 18/06/2026. The Head of Flying Operations suspended the evening Tarlton Springs service.

Damage and injuries

The aircraft sustained substantial damage:

  • three No. 2 propeller blades were damaged beyond limits, and the engine required a shock-load inspection
  • the right inboard flap had impact damage
  • the wing lower surface aft of the No. 2 nacelle was damaged
  • the right main gear doors were distorted
  • both right main tyres deflated through the fuse plugs, with brake energy at 84% of the certified maximum and no brake fire
  • the lower right fuselage was punctured

There were no serious injuries. One cabin crew member reported bruising during the disembarkation, and two kangaroos were killed.

Wreckage and survey

The runway survey recovered two kangaroo carcasses from runway 09, at 1,188 m and 1,221 m from the threshold, on and either side of the centreline. Continuous tyre marks ran from 1,160 m to the runway end, and the nose wheel rut continued 62 m beyond the end to the stopping point. The aircraft stopped 28 m short of the end of the prepared safety area, and the terrain beyond it is ungraded. A site inspection on 23/06/2026 found a continuous 140 m section of the northern perimeter fence with its bottom two wires separated from the posts, and an animal pad through it at the 1,050 m mark (Figure 3).

Personnel and organisational information

The operator's Operations Manual Part A 8.14.2 requires the pilot in command to request a runway inspection before the first departure after last light at an aerodrome listed in Appendix 8A, and not to start the take-off roll until the result is passed (Figure 1). Appendix 8A lists an aerodrome where a wildlife strike involving a company aircraft has been reported within the preceding 24 months. On 18/06/2026 it listed nine aerodromes, Tarlton Springs was not among them and had never been listed, and the list was last reviewed on 03/03/2025.

Part B 4.6.4 states that "At or above V1 the take-off shall be continued" (Figure 4). Part B appendix 4C bases its take-off data on failure of the critical engine at V1, automatic feathering of that propeller, an otherwise undamaged aeroplane and the operating engine at take-off power. The recurrent training syllabus TRG-SYL-07, module 4, scripts four scenarios: engine failure at 90 kt, engine fire at 100 kt, a configuration warning at 85 kt, and engine failure at V1 plus 5 kt, continued. Each is an aircraft system event.

Aerodrome Standard AS-139 10.4.2 requires a documented wildlife hazard management plan where an aerodrome is used by aeroplanes above 27,000 kg maximum take-off weight or serves more than 350,000 passenger movements a year. Tarlton Springs' heaviest scheduled aeroplane is 22,900 kg and it handled 61,400 passenger movements in 2025. The aerodrome held no such plan and is not in breach of the standard.

RRA-041 issue 3 (11/2022) is the current route risk assessment for Tarlton Springs and carries the operating restriction "daylight operations only pending review of night lighting and diversion fuel policy." Change Management Record CMR-2025-118, approved by the Head of Flying Operations on 22/05/2025, introduced one evening rotation from 14/07/2025. It was the first scheduled company operation into the aerodrome after last light. The change management record answered "No" to route risk assessment review required, and RRA-041 was not reopened.

Analysis

This analysis follows the chain from the aerodrome and operator conditions, through the departure, to the reject, the strike and the stop.

Organisation

The aerodrome operator met the standard that applied to it. Aerodrome Standard AS-139 section 10.4.1 provides that the operator of a certified aerodrome "must take reasonable measures to reduce the risk to aircraft operations presented by wildlife on or in the vicinity of the aerodrome". Section 10.4.2 requires a documented wildlife hazard management plan only "where the aerodrome is used by aeroplanes having a maximum take-off weight exceeding 27,000 kg, or serves more than 350,000 passenger movements in a calendar year". Section 10.4.3 provides that where 10.4.2 does not apply, the measures "need not be documented, but the aerodrome operator must be able to demonstrate what measures are in place".

Tarlton Springs' heaviest scheduled aeroplane is 22,900 kg and it handled 61,400 passenger movements in 2025, so neither limb applied and the aerodrome was not in breach. It held no plan, no hazard assessment and no dispersal programme. Its only documented measures were the single inspection before the first arrival under Aerodrome Manual 6.3 and a sighting log that nobody reviews.

With no plan, nothing owned the wildlife hazard as a hazard, and the northern perimeter fence sat in the works register as an ordinary maintenance item competing for council money. Item WR-221, raised in 04/2023, recorded four displaced panels and strained wire on the northern boundary between the 700 m and 1,300 m runway markers, with animals observed passing through. Replacement was estimated at $41,000. The item was deferred at the 2023, 2024 and 2025 budget rounds, each time as unfunded for review the next cycle, and item WR-263 in 02/2026 recorded the same section deteriorating further. The site inspection on 23/06/2026 found a continuous 140 m section with the bottom two wires separated from the posts, and a clear animal pad through it at the 1,050 m mark, 138 m before the point where the first carcass was recovered (Figure 2).

The pad and both carcasses are on the same side of the runway, and the register had recorded animals passing through this section since the day the item was raised. It is likely that the failed fence contributed to the two kangaroos reaching the sealed surface, because a fence repaired in 2023 would have left that section intact in 06/2026 and closed the one route the physical evidence shows. The evidence against this was weighed. The register recommends replacement without stating a specification, and kangaroos can clear a stock fence, so the pad shows that these two came through the gap but not that an intact fence would have stopped them. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether a replacement fence would exclude kangaroos] The sighting log also does not show where any of its 41 kangaroos came onto the aerodrome. [NOT ESTABLISHED: where the sighting log's kangaroos came onto the aerodrome] These points reduce confidence in the fence's contribution below certainty, but they do not displace the pad on the same side as the carcasses.

The standard's threshold bears on the fence in a different way. The deferrals were made with no hazard assessment in front of the council, which is what a plan would have put there, and a plan brings an owner and an audit. It is likely that the threshold, by leaving the aerodrome with no documented plan, contributed to the fence remaining unrepaired through three budget rounds. The Investigation held this conclusion with less confidence than the others in this chain, because 10.4.1 still obliged the operator to take reasonable measures. A documented plan is also not the only way to repair a fence, and the deferrals were budget decisions with no evidence that a plan would have attracted funding. The finding is that the threshold excused the aerodrome from the documentation that would have made the fence a recorded wildlife control, and that the fence stayed failed for that reason, as far as the evidence reaches.

The operator's own change management left a second condition in place. Route Risk Assessment RRA-041 issue 3 is the current assessment for Tarlton Springs and carries the operating restriction "daylight operations only pending review of night lighting and diversion fuel policy". Change Management Record CMR-2025-118, approved by the Head of Flying Operations on 22/05/2025, introduced a scheduled evening rotation from 14/07/2025. It assessed the change as "schedule change only", recorded "No new hazard identified", and answered "No" to "Route risk assessment review required". It did not reference the restriction, RRA-041 was not reopened and no issue 4 exists. The Safety Department's records show no involvement beyond receipt of the approved record.

The change created the first company operation into Tarlton Springs after last light, in contradiction of the restriction, through a process that asked whether the change was new rather than whether the assessment still held. SB512 was scheduled off blocks at 17:20 and began its roll at 17:30, five minutes after the end of civil twilight, so it departed in darkness because of the schedule and not because of a delay. A review that reopened RRA-041 would have had to assess a night operation at an aerodrome with a single runway, no lighting redundancy and no alternate within 200 nm at night. It is likely that the approval without review contributed to the roll in darkness. The restriction names night lighting and diversion fuel and not wildlife, so a review might have approved the evening service with conditions on those two items and left the departure after last light unchanged. The approver has left the company and cannot be asked what was in front of them. [NOT ESTABLISHED: why the approver assessed CMR-2025-118 as a schedule change only, because the approver has left the company] The connection is therefore to the darkness of the roll and not to the wildlife.

Environment

The log of wildlife sightings shows that the animals' presence at that hour was not a chance event. It holds 46 entries for 01/01/2025 to 18/06/2026, and 41 of them record kangaroos on or adjacent to the movement area. Of those 41, 38 are timed between one hour before and two hours after last light, and eleven record animals on the sealed surface of runway 09/27. On 18/06/2026 last light was 17:25, so the window ran from 16:25 to 19:25, and the roll began at 17:30 inside it. The pilot in command's account matches the log, because they had seen kangaroos on the strip at Tarlton Springs four or five times, always in the evening and never in daytime.

The log is a paper register, so it records sightings and not presence, and aerodrome staff go off duty at 18:30, part way through the window. The pattern may therefore partly reflect when somebody was there to see. [NOT ESTABLISHED: completeness of the sighting log, a paper register] Even so, the log and the pilot in command's account agree, and it is likely that departing in the logged peak contributed to the two kangaroos being on the runway at the roll.

Darkness then determined when the animals could be seen. The roll began at 17:30, 32 minutes after sunset at 16:58 and five minutes after the end of civil twilight at 17:25. Moonrise was not until 22:41 and the moon was 14% illuminated, so the strip had no natural ambient light and there was no town lighting in sight. The only lighting was the runway edge lighting the crew had switched on through the pilot-activated system at 17:21:50. The site visit at the same time of day on 23/06/2026 confirmed that the unlit graded strip either side of the sealed surface cannot be seen from the centreline.

The first officer estimated a range of around 200 m at first sight and called the animals at 17:30:31. After the stop the first officer said on the CVR that they "came out of the dark on the left of the strip, crossed the centreline", and added that there was "nothing to see and then there were two of them". The first officer later told the investigation that outside the lights it was black. The pilot in command was looking at the engine page after V1, which is where the procedure puts a pilot in command, so the sighting rested on the pilot flying.

In daylight, two animals crossing the graded strip from the northern fence would have been in view before they reached the seal and earlier in the roll. It is likely that the roll in darkness contributed to the late sighting and so to the reject at the point it was made. The Investigation held this conclusion lower than some others in the chain, for two reasons. The time the animals spent on the strip before reaching the seal is not known, and animals that arrived only seconds earlier would have been seen late in daylight too. [NOT ESTABLISHED: how long the animals were on the strip before reaching the seal] The pilot in command's position would also have been the same in daylight.

One further lighting matter could not be settled. A photometric check on 25/06/2026, seven days after the occurrence, measured four northern edge lights between the 900 m and 1,200 m markers at 118% to 131% of nominal intensity for stage 3, in the section the animals crossed. The remainder were within tolerance. The lighting is pilot-activated and runs for 30 minutes at one intensity set at the aerodrome's lighting controller, which was found at stage 3, the setting recorded at commissioning. Crews cannot vary it. The works register and electrical log show no work on the lighting or its controller between 18/06/2026 and the check, and the aerodrome's maintenance programme checks lamp serviceability but never measures intensity. It is therefore likely that the four lights were at the measured intensity on the night, although nobody measured them then.

Whether that intensity delayed detection of the animals, and so the reject, could equally have been so or not, and the evidence is evenly balanced. For it, the pilot in command recalled the lighting as brighter than they would want, a corridor of light with everything outside it black, so that anything off the seal could not be seen coming. Against it, the first officer, who saw the animals, described the lighting as normal and saw them clearly on the seal at around 200 m, although with only two daylight landings to compare against they were not well placed to judge. The pilot in command's non-detection has an explanation that does not need the lighting, because they were looking at the engine page. Darkness alone explains why nothing off the seal was seen, and nothing available links a 131% edge light to the detection of an animal. A study of lighting contrast and animal detection would be needed to settle it. The matter remains unresolved and is not carried into the findings.

Procedures

The operator had a control aimed at exactly this hazard, and it would have worked had it applied. Operations Manual Part A 8.14.2 provides that "At an aerodrome listed in Appendix 8A, the pilot in command shall request a runway inspection from the aerodrome operator prior to the first departure after last light, and shall not commence the take-off roll until the result of that inspection has been passed". Section 8.14.3 provides that "At all other aerodromes, no specific action is required". Appendix 8A lists an aerodrome only "where a wildlife strike involving a company aircraft has been reported at that aerodrome within the preceding 24 months" (Figure 1).

Nine aerodromes were listed on 18/06/2026. Tarlton Springs was not among them and had never been listed, so it never met the condition. No provision in Part A asks a crew to report a sighting, and no provision admits an aerodrome to the list on any other evidence. The list was last reviewed on 03/03/2025, four months before the evening service began. The eleven sightings of kangaroos on the sealed surface could not put the aerodrome on the list, because they were not strikes and were not reported to the company. The criterion could therefore only be met by the outcome the inspection exists to prevent.

It is very likely that this listing criterion led to no inspection being requested before the departure after last light. An inspection some minutes before the roll cannot guarantee a clear runway at the roll, which is the reason the conclusion stops short of certainty. The aerodrome's staff disperse animals when they find them, so a requirement that applied at Tarlton Springs would have required a request and a pass before the roll.

The omission itself is well supported. Neither the CVR nor the aerodrome's CTAF recording contains a request for a runway inspection, an offer of one, or any mention of wildlife before departure, and the pilot in command said wildlife was not discussed with anyone during the turnaround. The only inspection that day was at 07:35, before the first arrival, with the result "movement area clear". Aerodrome Manual 6.3 provides for inspections outside the scheduled time on request, and the reporting officer, who was on duty at the terminal during the turnaround, confirmed that one would have been carried out if asked. SB512 was the only departure after last light that day.

Both crew stated that they did not consider an inspection. The pilot in command had expected Tarlton Springs to be on the Appendix 8A list and was surprised to find it was not, and in their air safety report the pilot in command said no company document prompted them to think about it. An inspection would have covered the 1,050 m to 1,250 m section, where the fence pad and both carcasses were found. It is likely that the omission contributed to the animals being on the runway at the roll. The Investigation did not attribute the omission to either crew member individually, because no document gave the step to anyone.

The same pattern appears in the guidance for the decision that followed. Part B 4.6.4 states "At or above V1 the take-off shall be continued. The decision to continue is made before V1 is reached" (Figure 4). Section 4.6 contains no guidance on an obstruction seen on the runway at any speed, and no amplification of 4.6.4 for a case in which continuing is itself hazardous. Recurrent training syllabus TRG-SYL-07 module 4 has four scripted scenarios: engine failure at 90 kt, engine fire at 100 kt, configuration warning at 85 kt, and engine failure at V1 plus 5 kt, continued. All four are aircraft system events and none presents an obstruction, an animal or any external hazard on the runway. No crew has been presented with an external obstruction scenario in the five cycles on file, and 214 crew completed the module in the current cycle. [NOT ESTABLISHED: training scenario records beyond the five cycles on file]

Both the pilot in command and the first officer stated independently that every stop or go scenario they had been given was an engine event. Part B appendix 4C states the basis of the V1 rule's go case as the "failure of the critical engine", "automatic feathering of the propeller of the failed engine" and "an aeroplane otherwise undamaged". Neither Part B 4.6 nor the syllabus tells a crew that an obstruction struck at or after V1 can remove several of those assumptions at once.

The pilot in command stated that they knew the rule and departed from it deliberately, so training would not have changed what they knew. They did not reject because they were untrained but because they judged the alternative worse. Against that, an unrehearsed decision made in about a second is not the same as one made against a briefed and practised frame. A third reading comes from the performance assessment, which indicates that guidance could only have told the crew which of two outcomes outside the certified data to take. It is likely that the absence of training and guidance for an obstruction during the take-off roll contributed to the take-off being rejected above V1. That conclusion rests on the decision being unrehearsed, not on what guidance would have said.

People

The flight data recorder shows V1 called at 112 kt at 17:30:29 and both power levers retarded to flight idle from 17:30:32 at 118 kt, three seconds and six knots past V1. The CVR holds the whole decision in one exchange (Figure 5). The first officer called the animals at 17:30:31 and the pilot in command said "Stopping. I have control." at 17:30:32. Part B 4.6.4 required the take-off to be continued. In interview and in their air safety report, the pilot in command said they judged that rotating into two large animals would leave the aircraft airborne at night with damage they could not assess, over country with no usable option. They took the risk whose end they could see and said plainly that it was not by the book.

The late start of the stop is why the stop did not fit the runway. The scheduled accelerate-stop distance required was 1,780 m against an accelerate-stop distance available of 1,847 m, a margin of 67 m, and it assumes the stop begins at or before V1. The reject began at about 1,152 m, leaving 695 m of sealed surface. Beginning the stop six knots and three seconds late consumes the 67 m margin and more. It is extremely likely that the reject above V1 contributed to the overrun, because a continued take-off would not have run off the end of the runway.

Whether continuing would have been worse is a separate question. Performance assessment PEA-2026-0417 reconstructs a continued take-off from the same point, and its result bears on how the decision should be read. The aircraft would have reached the animals at the same place within a few hundredths of a second of the actual time, rotating at about 120 kt and 4 to 5 degrees nose-up with the main wheels on the runway. The No. 2 propeller tip would have been about 1.3 m above the runway against a measured standing height of 1.6 m for the larger animal, and a strike on the No. 2 propeller and right main gear is assessed as close to certain, at take-off power.

The propeller teardown PTR-2026-0417-02 found the pitch change actuator cracked through and its oil lost. The same damage that stopped the No. 2 reverse would also have stopped the propeller feathering. With the propeller windmilling, the right main gear doors unable to close and the right inboard flap damaged, the central case gives a one-engine gross climb gradient of 1.0% against the 2.4% minimum, with the net path about 55 ft below the top of the mast and 35 ft not reached until about 520 m beyond the runway end. The mast is 184 ft high and 3,400 m beyond the end of runway 09 (Figure 6). The most favourable ends of every range give 1.9% gross, still short of the clearance required, and with the gear left down there is no climb. The one damaged case above the minimum needs a feather that the teardown says was not possible, and it would leave about 3.2% gross. Beyond the mast, no alternate exists within 200 nm at night, so the aircraft would have had to return at night over unlit country to a runway with two carcasses on it.

On that reconstruction, rejecting the take-off was likely the safest course of action available. It is held at likely and no higher. The reconstruction works from damage done at flight idle and 114 kt, and the teardown report notes that at take-off power and a higher speed the propeller would have absorbed more energy and that it cannot say whether the pitch change mechanism would have failed in the same way. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the pitch change mechanism would have failed in the same way at take-off power] A gradient below the minimum is also not a crash.

Several matters about the continued case were not assessed or could not be established. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the right inboard flap would have retracted past the torn fairing] [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the right main gear leg would have reached its uplock with the door fouled] [NOT ESTABLISHED: what sustained No. 2 propeller imbalance would have done to the engine mounts and nacelle] [NOT ESTABLISHED: controllability at V2 with the right flap damaged and the right propeller windmilling]

This assessment does not lower the reject's contribution to the overrun. It does not make the decision compliant with Part B 4.6.4, and it does not show that the pilot in command could have known it in the second available.

The response after the decision worked well. Power levers reached flight idle 0.6 seconds after the decision, and maximum braking was established at 17:30:34, two seconds after it, against a fleet mean of 3.2 seconds from decision to maximum braking. Anti-skid was active on all four wheels throughout, and brake energy reached 84% of the certified maximum without a brake fire. The first officer made the speed callouts and the runway-end call. A stop begun at the fleet mean response would have carried the aircraft an estimated further 30 to 40 m, close to the far edge of the runway end safety area. It is very likely that the prompt braking reduced the risk, because it kept the overrun to 62 m into a prepared surface at low speed.

One matter bearing on the crew's condition could not be settled. The take-off was 11 hours into the duty, on the fifth sector, after a 06:30 sign-on. The day had been extended that morning from three sectors to five when the crew picked up the evening rotation from a crew member who reported unfit. Both crew described themselves as tired at that point, and the pilot in command said they would have declined another sector. Against that, both described the tiredness as ordinary and not impairing.

The duty was inside the company's limits, planned at 13 hours against a 13 hour 30 minute maximum, and the pilot in command's duty and rest in the previous seven days were within limits with no variations applied. The recorded performance shows none of the usual signs of impairment. The levers reached flight idle in 0.6 seconds, braking was established at the fast end of the fleet's distribution, the callouts were made on time, and there is no error of omission on the roll. A tired state is not the same as fatigue to a degree that degrades performance, so whether the crew were fatigued is about as likely as not, and it could not be determined either way. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the crew were fatigued] Settling it would need a detailed fatigue assessment with sleep history and the duty pattern before 18/06/2026. That was judged not required, because every mechanism fatigue would have worked through here is contradicted by recorded data, and the one decision it could plausibly have touched, the inspection request, was never prompted by any document. The matter remains unresolved and is not carried into the findings.

Equipment

The animals' presence on the runway led to the strike through the aircraft's own geometry. The first officer's call, the impact and the two carcasses each show that the animals were on the sealed surface. Two adult kangaroos were recovered on and either side of the centreline at 1,188 m and 1,221 m from the threshold, with the animal pad through the northern fence at 1,050 m (Figure 3). It is extremely likely that the kangaroos reaching the runway led to both the reject and the strike. The first officer's call at 17:30:31 is the only trigger for the reject on the CVR, and the impact followed at 17:30:33.

The impact came at 114 kt, one second after the reject began, with both engines already near flight idle at 12% and 9% torque. The flight data recorder shows a lateral acceleration spike of 0.31 g right and a vertical spike of 1.48 g. Three No. 2 propeller blades were damaged beyond repairable limits, with one blade tip separated, and animal tissue was recovered from two blade roots. The pitch change actuator was cracked through and its oil lost, so the blades could not be driven to ground idle or reverse. The No. 2 reverse interlock did not make, and the No. 2 propeller stayed near flight idle for the rest of the stop.

Remains and debris crushed the lower skin of the right inboard flap over 0.9 m of span and holed the wing lower surface aft of the nacelle. The right main gear doors were distorted, with the forward door bowed 85 mm against a 22 mm clearance, and propeller debris punctured the lower right fuselage skin. Both right main tyres deflated through the fuse plugs, consistent with brake energy. The damage to the flap, doors and fuselage did not bear on the stop beyond the reverse.

The scheduled accelerate-stop figures take no credit for reverse thrust but assume both propellers at ground idle, whose disc drag is part of the certified deceleration. With the No. 2 propeller unable to reach ground idle and reverse on No. 1 only, held straight with rudder, the mean deceleration from maximum braking was 2.6 m/s2, approximately 15% below the value used in the certified data. This is stated plainly. The stopping distance achieved from 118 kt was 757 m against the 695 m available. At the certified deceleration from the same point, the reconstruction puts the stop at roughly 660 m, inside the runway remaining.

Neither contribution alone would have brought the aircraft to the end. The late start of the stop left 695 m, and the reduced deceleration then needed 757 m. The aircraft left the seal at 17:30:51 at 21 kt, where deceleration fell to 1.9 m/s2 in graded gravel. It stopped at 17:30:57, upright and on the extended centreline, 62 m into the 90 m runway end safety area and 28 m short of the end of the prepared surface. There was no fire.

Other factors that increased risk

Two factors failed the test of influence on this occurrence but carry risk that remains.

The evening rotation was rostered to close five-sector duties within 45 minutes of the limit. The rostering extract for 14/07/2025 to 18/06/2026 shows the rotation operated on 289 days, each time as the fourth and fifth sectors of a Port Carrick-based duty signing on between 06:00 and 07:00. Planned duty was between 12 hours 45 minutes and 13 hours 15 minutes, against a 13 hour 30 minute maximum. On six of those days a member of the rostered crew reported unfit and the rotation went to a crew already on duty, extending that crew's day from three sectors to five, and 18/06/2026 was the sixth. The roster therefore puts the last sector of the longest duty in the pattern into an aerodrome that RRA-041 records as having no alternate within 200 nm at night and limited engineering support.

It is unlikely that the roster contributed to this occurrence. The flight data recorder response was at the fast end of the fleet's distribution and there was no error of omission on the roll. The one decision a long duty could plausibly have affected, the inspection request, was never available to be affected, because no document prompted either crew member to consider it. Whether the crew were fatigued is itself unsettled. Even so, the exposure is a standing one in the roster that is present on every operation of the rotation, so the Investigation found it likely to be important as a risk, and it is a safety issue in its own right.

The checking of floor proximity escape path lighting is the second. The pre-flight emergency lighting test on this type illuminates the ceiling emergency lights and the exit signs, but it neither illuminates nor monitors the floor proximity segments. Their only check is a dedicated functional test at the maintenance programme's 24-month interval. The first officer noticed sections of the aisle floor strip unlit while walking back through the cabin during the disembarkation. The functional check on 24/06/2026 found two of the six floor proximity segments on the left side aft of row 16 dark on battery power with the system armed, traced to a failed common ballast. The last dedicated functional test had been 11 months before the occurrence, within the interval, so neither the crew nor a line engineer could have detected the defect.

It is unlikely that this gap affected the overrun or its outcome. No evacuation was commanded, the main cabin lights were on throughout, and the disembarkation by the forward airstair took 4 minutes 8 seconds without incident. The matter remains under examination, and as it stands the gap is very likely to be important as a risk. Between functional tests the state of the escape path lighting on any aircraft of the type is unknown, and the defect on VH-SBQ could have stayed hidden for up to 13 more months. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the same ballast part is fitted across the fleet]

Hypotheses tested and excluded

Two hypotheses were tested and not supported. A tailwind during the roll and stop was very unlikely, because the automatic weather station gave 090 at 7, 6 and 5 kt at the 16:30, 17:00 and 18:00 observations, a headwind component of 5 to 7 kt on runway 09. The recorded wind during the roll gave a headwind component of 4 to 6 kt throughout, and the crew's performance entry used 5 kt. A No. 2 engine power loss before the reject decision was also very unlikely. Both engines held 98.4% and 98.5% torque until the levers were retarded at 17:30:32, with fuel flow, ITT and propeller RPM normal and no caution, warning or exceedance recorded. The borescope found no pre-existing damage, the pilot in command's first words on the CVR were "Stopping. I have control.", and the No. 2 damage and RPM decay began at 17:30:33, after the reject and at impact.

Findings summary

This investigation applied "Likely or probable": a proposition is established at a probability of 65% or more and not established at 35% or less, and anything between is inconclusive.

Times in this report are local time (UTC+10).

Contributing factors

  1. The take-off was rejected at 118 kt, 6 kt above V1, and this virtually certainly occurred. It was extremely likely, and so very likely, to have contributed to the overrun because the 67 m margin between the scheduled accelerate-stop distance and the accelerate-stop distance available was consumed by a stop begun three seconds after V1.
  2. Two kangaroos crossed the strip onto the sealed runway, which is virtually certain. It was very likely that this contributed to the occurrence, because the reject and the strike both followed from the animals being on the surface.
  3. The No. 2 propeller and the right main gear struck the two kangaroos, which is virtually certain. This virtually certainly contributed to the overrun, because the strike took the No. 2 propeller out of the stop.
  4. The deceleration achieved was below the scheduled accelerate-stop performance, which is virtually certain. This virtually certainly contributed to the overrun, because the stop needed 757 m against 695 m of sealed runway remaining.
  5. The take-off roll began in darkness, 5 minutes after last light with no moon, which is virtually certain. It was likely that this contributed to the reject, because the strip either side of the sealed surface could not be seen from the centreline.
  6. The departure fell within the logged kangaroo peak, from one hour before to two hours after last light. This was very likely the case, and it was likely that it contributed, because 38 of the 41 logged kangaroo sightings fell in that window.
  7. No runway inspection was requested before the departure after last light, which is virtually certain. It was likely that this contributed, because an inspection would have covered the section of runway where the animals were later found.
  8. The operator's requirement for a runway inspection before the first departure after last light applied only at aerodromes listed in Appendix 8A, and an aerodrome could be listed only after a wildlife strike involving a company aircraft had been reported there in the preceding 24 months. This is virtually certain, and it was very likely that it contributed, because Tarlton Springs was not listed and no inspection was requested. (Safety Issue)
  9. Neither the training syllabus nor the Operations Manual gave crews any scenario or guidance for an obstruction on the runway during the take-off roll. This was very likely the case, and it was likely that it contributed to the reject at 118 kt. (Safety Issue)
  10. The evening service into Tarlton Springs was approved without reopening the route risk assessment that restricted the aerodrome to daylight operations. This is virtually certain, and it was likely that it contributed, because it led to the departure after last light. (Safety Issue)
  11. The failed northern boundary fence was left unrepaired through three budget rounds, which is virtually certain. It was likely that this contributed, because the failed section was the route by which the animals reached the movement area. (Safety Issue)
  12. The Aerodrome Standard AS-139 threshold for a documented wildlife hazard management plan left Tarlton Springs with no such plan, which is virtually certain. It was likely that this contributed, because without a plan the fence repair remained a deferrable works item with no hazard assessment behind it. (Safety Issue)

Other factors that increased risk

  1. The evening rotation was rostered to close five-sector duties within 45 minutes of the maximum permitted duty, which is virtually certain. It was unlikely to have influenced this occurrence, but it was likely to have increased risk on every operation of the rotation. (Safety Issue)
  2. The floor proximity escape path lighting on this aircraft type is checked only by a functional test at a 24-month interval and not pre-flight. This was virtually certain on the evidence so far, and the matter is still being examined. It was unlikely to have influenced this occurrence, and it was very likely to have increased risk because the gap left a defect on VH-SBQ undetected. (Safety Issue)

Other findings

  1. Maximum braking was established within 2 seconds of the reject decision, against a fleet mean of 3.2 seconds. This is virtually certain, and it was very likely that it decreased risk, because the aircraft stopped 62 m into the 90 m runway end safety area at low speed.
  2. A tailwind component during the take-off roll and stop was very unlikely, because both the aerodrome observations and the recorded aircraft data showed a headwind throughout.
  3. A No. 2 engine power loss before the reject decision was very unlikely, because both engines were within 0.1% torque of each other until the power levers were retarded, and the No. 2 propeller damage began after the reject at the moment of impact.
  4. The aerodrome operator was not in breach of AS-139 section 10.4, because neither limb of 10.4.2 applied to Tarlton Springs.
  5. On the reconstruction of a continued take-off, rejecting the take-off was probably the safest course of action available. This does not lessen the reject's contribution to the overrun, does not make the decision compliant with Part B 4.6.4, and does not show that the pilot in command could have known it in the second available.

Safety actions

  • The Head of Flying Operations suspended the evening Tarlton Springs service on 19/06/2026.
  • The operator amended Appendix 8A by temporary revision TR-2026-04 on 26/06/2026 to list Tarlton Springs, so the Part A 8.14.2 inspection requirement applies to every departure there after last light pending a permanent change.
  • The aerodrome operator funded works register item WR-221 and programmed the replacement of the 140 m northern boundary fence for 09/2026, and installed a temporary electric wire on 25/06/2026.
  • Recommendation 1: that the operator replace the Appendix 8A listing criterion so an aerodrome is listed on wildlife exposure rather than on a reported strike, and add a route risk assessment trigger for any aerodrome first operated into after last light. A response is due by 30/09/2026.
  • Recommendation 2: that the operator, with the type certificate holder, develop guidance and simulator training for an obstruction on the runway during the take-off roll, including at and after V1. A response is due by 30/09/2026.

Appendix B: Excluded hypotheses

Two hypotheses were tested and were not supported. Each is retained here with the evidence against it.

Tailwind component during the take-off roll and stop. The hypothesis was tested because a stop that ran 62 m past the runway end invites a question about the wind. It was very unlikely that a tailwind existed.

  • The aerodrome's automatic weather station observations at 16:30, 17:00 and 18:00 gave wind from 090 at 7, 6 and 5 kt, a headwind component of 5 to 7 kt on runway 09.
  • The recorded wind during the roll gave a headwind component of 4 to 6 kt throughout, with no tailwind component at any point.
  • The crew's performance entry used a 5 kt headwind, which matches both sources.

No. 2 engine power loss before the reject decision. The hypothesis was tested because a reject at 118 kt is most commonly an engine event. It was very unlikely that a power loss preceded the reject.

  • The FDR recorded both engines at 98.4% and 98.5% torque, within 0.1% of each other, from power set at 17:30:02 until the power levers were retarded at 17:30:32. Fuel flow, ITT and propeller RPM on both engines stayed within normal scatter.
  • No caution, warning or exceedance was recorded before the reject.
  • The CVR contains no engine-related call. The pilot in command's first words were "Stopping. I have control." one second after the first officer's sighting call.
  • The borescope inspection of both engines found no pre-existing damage.
  • The No. 2 propeller damage and the RPM decay both began at 17:30:33, after the reject and at the moment of impact. The loss of No. 2 power was therefore a consequence of the strike and not a cause of the reject.

  • "10.4.1 The operator of a certified aerodrome must take reasonable measures to reduce the risk to aircraft operations presented by wildlife on or in the vicinity of the aerodrome."
  • "10.4.2 The operator of a certified aerodrome must prepare, implement and maintain a documented wildlife hazard management plan where the aerodrome is used by aeroplanes having a maximum take-off weight exceeding 27,000 kg, or serves more than 350,000 passenger movements in a calendar year."
  • "10.4.3 Where subsection 10.4.2 does not apply, the measures taken under 10.4.1 need not be documented, but the aerodrome operator must be able to demonstrate what measures are in place."

Tarlton Springs is a certified aerodrome. Its heaviest scheduled aeroplane is the 22,900 kg twin-turboprop used on the Saltbush Air service, and it handled 61,400 passenger movements in 2025. Section 10.4.2 therefore did not apply to it, it held no wildlife hazard management plan, and it was not in breach of the standard.

Operations Manual Part A 8.14 and Appendix 8A

The text is from revision 9, dated 04/2024 (Figure 1). Section 8.14.2 states: "At an aerodrome listed in Appendix 8A, the pilot in command shall request a runway inspection from the aerodrome operator prior to the first departure after last light, and shall not commence the take-off roll until the result of that inspection has been passed." Section 8.14.3 states: "At all other aerodromes, no specific action is required. Crews should remain alert to the possibility of wildlife on the movement area." Section 8.14.4 requires a wildlife strike to be reported on an air safety report, after which the Safety Department reviews the aerodrome's status against the Appendix 8A criteria.

Appendix 8A states: "An aerodrome is listed in this appendix where a wildlife strike involving a company aircraft has been reported at that aerodrome within the preceding 24 months. The list is reviewed annually by the Safety Department." As current on 18/06/2026 it listed nine aerodromes. Tarlton Springs was not among them and had never been listed. The list was last reviewed on 03/03/2025. A sighting cannot put an aerodrome on the list, and nothing in Part A asks a crew to report one.

Operations Manual Part B 4.6 and appendix 4C

Section 4.6 is from revision 14, dated 09/2025 (Figure 4). Section 4.6.2 states: "Below 80 kt the take-off shall be rejected for any malfunction or condition that in the judgement of the pilot in command makes the aircraft unfit to fly." Section 4.6.3 limits rejection between 80 kt and V1 to fire or fire warning, engine failure, a configuration warning, loss of directional control, or the pilot in command's judgement that the aircraft is unsafe or unable to fly. Section 4.6.4 states: "At or above V1 the take-off shall be continued. The decision to continue is made before V1 is reached." The section contains no guidance on an obstruction seen on the runway at any speed, and no amplification of 4.6.4 for a case in which continuing is itself hazardous.

Appendix 4C, from the same revision, takes its speeds, distances and climb gradients from the Aeroplane Flight Manual. It assumes failure of the critical engine at the engine failure speed VEF recognised by V1, automatic feathering of the failed engine's propeller, and an aeroplane "otherwise undamaged and in the take-off configuration". It also assumes the landing gear retracted once a positive rate of climb is established, take-off flap held to acceleration altitude, and the operating engine at take-off power. Section 4C.4 states that "the minimum gross climb gradient with one engine inoperative, take-off flap set and the landing gear retracted is 2.4%". The net flight path is the gross path reduced by 0.8% and must clear every obstacle in the take-off funnel by 35 ft. Section 4C.9 records a telecommunications mast with its top 184 ft above aerodrome elevation, 3,400 m beyond the end of runway 09 and 260 m north of the extended centreline. The appendix says nothing about applying the data to an aircraft damaged during the take-off roll, and Part B 4.6 does not refer to its assumptions.

Route Risk Assessment RRA-041 and Change Management Record CMR-2025-118

RRA-041 issue 3, dated 11/2022, is the current issue and no issue 4 exists. It assessed hazards including a single runway with no lighting redundancy, no alternate within 200 nm at night, and limited engineering support. It carries the operating restriction: "daylight operations only pending review of night lighting and diversion fuel policy."

CMR-2025-118, "Introduction of the Tarlton Springs evening service", was approved on 22/05/2025 by the Head of Flying Operations. Its scope was the "addition of one evening rotation, Port Carrick to Tarlton Springs to Port Carrick, six days per week, from 14/07/2025." Its assessment read: "schedule change only. Existing aerodrome, existing aircraft type, existing crew qualifications, existing engineering support arrangements. No new hazard identified." It answered "No" to route risk assessment review required. The change introduced the first scheduled operation into Tarlton Springs after last light. The daylight-only restriction is not referenced anywhere in CMR-2025-118, RRA-041 was not reopened, and the Safety Department's records show no involvement beyond receipt of the approved record.

Recurrent training syllabus TRG-SYL-07, module 4

The module belongs to the 2025 to 2026 cycle. Its objective states that "the crew will demonstrate a correctly executed rejected take-off for an engine failure, an engine fire and a configuration warning, each initiated below V1, and will demonstrate the decision to continue for a failure recognised at or after V1." The four scripted simulator scenarios are engine failure at 90 kt, engine fire at 100 kt, configuration warning at 85 kt, and engine failure at V1 plus 5 kt, continued. Every scenario is an aircraft system event, and none presents an obstruction, an animal or any external hazard on the runway at any speed. The company's training records show 214 crew completed module 4 in the 2025 to 2026 cycle, and no crew has been presented with an external obstruction scenario in the five cycles held on file.

Wildlife sighting log (summary)

The log is a paper register held in the aerodrome office and was copied on 23/06/2026, covering 01/01/2025 to 18/06/2026. It holds 46 entries, of which 41 record kangaroos on or adjacent to the movement area. Of those 41, 38 are timed between one hour before and two hours after last light, and eleven record animals on the sealed surface of runway 09/27. The log is not reported to any operator, and the aerodrome reporting officer confirmed that no airline has ever asked for it.

Works register WR-221 and WR-263 (summary)

Item WR-221 in the Tarlton Shire Council aerodrome works register was raised in 04/2023. It records four displaced panels and strained wire on the northern perimeter fence between the 700 m and 1,300 m runway markers, with animals observed passing through, and an estimated replacement cost of $41,000. It was deferred at the 2023, 2024 and 2025 budget rounds, each entry recording the item as deferred, unfunded and for review in the next cycle. Item WR-263, raised in 02/2026, records the same section as deteriorating further. The site inspection on 23/06/2026 found a continuous 140 m section of the northern fence with the bottom two wires separated from the posts, and a clear animal pad through it at the 1,050 m mark.

Post-occurrence inspection report (summary)

The engineering inspection of VH-SBQ was carried out from 19/06/2026 to 21/06/2026.

  • No. 2 propeller: Three blades were damaged beyond repairable limits, with leading edge deformation and one blade tip separated. Animal tissue was recovered from two blade roots. The engine was subject to a shock-load inspection, and the borescope of both engines found no pre-existing damage and no evidence of a power anomaly before the impact.
  • Right main landing gear: Both tyres had deflated through the fuse plugs, consistent with brake energy. The gear doors were distorted by impact, and the gear structure was within limits.
  • Brakes: The brake energy absorbed was calculated at 84% of the certified maximum. There was no brake fire and no hydraulic leak, and the anti-skid system tested serviceable.
  • Lower right fuselage skin: There was abrasion and two punctures consistent with propeller debris.
  • Right wing and inboard flap: The inboard flap was damaged and the wing lower surface had two punctures aft of the No. 2 nacelle, with animal tissue in the flap damage. These were referred for the structural survey.
  • Runway and RESA survey: Two animal carcasses were recovered at 1,188 m and 1,221 m from the runway 09 threshold. Continuous tyre marks ran from 1,160 m to the runway end. The nose wheel rut ran in the RESA to 62 m beyond the end, on the extended centreline.

Structures report ESR-2026-0417 and propeller teardown PTR-2026-0417-02 (summary)

ESR-2026-0417 records the structural survey of VH-SBQ on jacks at Tarlton Springs from 26/06/2026 to 28/06/2026 and was issued on 29/06/2026. The propeller overhaul contractor's teardown report PTR-2026-0417-02 was issued on 30/06/2026.

  • Strike damage and overrun damage were separated by animal tissue and hair, the direction of deformation and the absence of gravel. Overrun damage is confined to the nose gear, its doors and the lower forward fuselage.
  • The right inboard flap, at the take-off setting at impact, had its lower skin crushed and torn over 0.9 m of span outboard of the nacelle. Its trailing edge was deformed upward by up to 40 mm, the vane leading edge was dented in three places, and the outboard flap track fairing was torn away. The report could not establish whether the flap would have retracted past the torn fairing, and records that flap asymmetry protection would have stopped both flaps if it had not.
  • The right wing lower surface aft of the No. 2 nacelle had two punctures of 30 mm and 55 mm consistent with propeller debris, with no main spar damage and no fuel leak.
  • The forward right main gear door was bowed 85 mm outboard at its trailing edge against a running clearance to the nacelle of 22 mm, and the aft door's hinge line was displaced. The forward door moves with the gear leg, so it would have met the nacelle structure on retraction. The report assesses gear retraction as possible but not assured and door closure as not possible, and could not establish whether the leg would have reached its uplock with the door fouled.
  • The No. 2 pitch change actuator dome was cracked through, the oil transfer tube was fractured, and the pitch change oil was lost. With the actuator breached the blades cannot be driven to feather or into the ground and reverse range, and the pitch lock holds them near the angle they had when oil pressure was lost. The report gives this as the reason the No. 2 reverse interlock did not make and states that the propeller could not have been feathered after the impact.
  • With one blade tip gone the propeller is severely out of balance while it turns. The teardown report did not assess what sustained imbalance would have done to the engine mounts or the nacelle.
  • All of the damage was done at flight idle and 114 kt. The teardown report notes that at take-off power and a higher speed the propeller would have absorbed more energy at impact, and that it cannot say whether the pitch change mechanism would have failed in the same way.

Performance assessment PEA-2026-0417 (summary)

Saltbush Air Performance Engineering issued the assessment on 01/07/2026, using the type certificate holder's drag data for the damage in ESR-2026-0417. It reconstructs a take-off continued at 17:30:32 and states that it is a reconstruction of something that did not happen.

VR, 116 kt, was reached at 17:30:31, the second of the sighting call, and no rotate call was made. A continued take-off would have rotated from about 17:30:31.5 at the operator's normal rate of about 3 degrees a second. From the reject point at 1,152 m, a continued aircraft still accelerating at about 2 kt a second would have reached the impact point, about 1,210 m, within a few hundredths of a second of the time the aircraft actually did. It would have been at about 120 kt and 4 to 5 degrees nose-up, with the main wheels still on the runway, and liftoff would have followed at about 17:30:34, about 1,300 m along the runway. At that attitude the No. 2 propeller tip would have been about 1.3 m above the runway, against a measured standing height of 1.6 m for the larger animal. A strike on the No. 2 propeller and the right main gear was assessed as close to certain, at take-off power rather than flight idle.

For the undamaged aircraft at 20,800 kg, flap 10, 412 ft and +8 °C, the one-engine-inoperative second-segment gradient was 4.1% gross and 3.3% net with the propeller feathered and the gear up, against the 2.4% minimum. The take-off was limited by accelerate-stop distance and not by climb. The gross gradient penalties for departures from the appendix 4C basis were as follows, with the range in brackets.

  • No. 2 propeller unfeathered and windmilling at the pitch-lock angle, engine shut down: 2.2% (1.6% to 2.8%).
  • Right main gear retracted with doors unable to close: 0.4% (0.3% to 0.5%).
  • Right main gear not retracted, in place of the line above: 1.6% (1.4% to 1.8%).
  • Right inboard flap damage, with the roll control needed to hold the wings level: 0.5% (0.3% to 0.8%).

The one damaged case above the minimum needs a feather that the teardown says was not possible. Controllability at V2 with the right flap damaged and the right propeller windmilling, and the effect of the propeller's imbalance, were not assessed. The assessment notes that RRA-041 records no alternate within 200 nm at night, so a continued aircraft would have had to return to Tarlton Springs at night over unlit country, to a runway with the two carcasses on it.

Crew and duty records, 18/06/2026

The pilot in command had 8,410 total hours, 2,140 on type, and 3 years 1 month in command. The last cyclic simulator was on 11/03/2026 and the last line check on 02/12/2025, both satisfactory. There was no prior occurrence history, and duty and rest in the 7 days before the occurrence were within the company's limits with no variations applied.

The first officer had 1,655 total hours, 405 on type, and 14 months with the company. The last cyclic simulator was on 28/04/2026, with all items satisfactory. The first officer had flown two prior sectors into Tarlton Springs, both in daylight, on 09/01/2026 and 17/02/2026.

The duty began at 06:30 with five sectors. The first three, Port Carrick to Hensby, Hensby to Mardle Creek and Mardle Creek to Port Carrick, were rostered. SB511 Port Carrick to Tarlton Springs and SB512 Tarlton Springs to Port Carrick were added on the morning of 18/06/2026 when a member of the rostered crew reported unfit. The occurrence at 17:30 was 11 hours 00 minutes into a duty planned to finish at 19:30, with SB512 scheduled on blocks in Port Carrick at 19:15. That gave a planned duty of 13 hours 00 minutes against a maximum of 13 hours 30 minutes for five sectors with this sign-on under the company's approved fatigue risk management system. A ground delay in Port Carrick during the third sector was recovered on the Tarlton Springs turnaround. SB512 was scheduled off blocks at 17:20, the doors closed at 17:16, and it departed on schedule.

The rostering system extract for 14/07/2025 to 18/06/2026 shows the evening rotation operated on 289 days. Each time it was rostered as the fourth and fifth sectors of a Port Carrick-based duty signing on between 06:00 and 07:00, planned at between 12 hours 45 minutes and 13 hours 15 minutes. On six of those days a member of the rostered crew reported unfit and the rotation was reassigned to a crew already on duty, extending that crew's day from three sectors to five. 18/06/2026 was the sixth.

Photometric check of edge lighting, 25/06/2026 (summary)

The check was carried out at the investigator's request. The runway lighting is pilot-activated. It is keyed from the CTAF and runs for 30 minutes at the single intensity set at the aerodrome's lighting controller, which was found at stage 3, the highest of the fittings' three stages and the setting recorded at commissioning. Crews cannot vary it. Four northern runway 09/27 edge lights between the 900 m and 1,200 m markers measured between 118% and 131% of the nominal intensity for stage 3, and the remainder were within tolerance. The works register and electrical log record no work on the runway lighting or its controller between 18/06/2026 and the check. The aerodrome operator's maintenance programme checks lamp serviceability but does not measure intensity.

Cabin emergency lighting functional check, 24/06/2026 (summary)

The check was raised following the first officer's account. With the emergency lighting system armed and the aircraft on battery power, two of the six floor proximity escape path segments on the left side aft of row 16 did not illuminate. The fault was traced to a failed ballast common to both segments. The pre-flight emergency lighting test on this type illuminates the ceiling emergency lights and the exit signs and does not illuminate or monitor the floor proximity segments. The defect was therefore not detectable by any check available to the crew or a line engineer without a dedicated functional test. The last dedicated functional test was 11 months before the occurrence, within the maintenance programme's 24-month interval. The disembarkation was conducted with the main cabin lights on, by the forward airstair, without urgency.

Appendix E: Figures

The site inspection on 23/06/2026 photographed the failed section of the northern perimeter fence and the animal pad through it at the 1,050 m mark (Figure 2).

The runway survey and the FDR distance reconstruction place the animal pad through the failed fence at 1,050 m, the reject point at 1,152 m, the carcasses at 1,188 m and 1,221 m, and the stop 62 m beyond the runway end on one line from the threshold (Figure 3).

The performance assessment's gross and net climb paths for a continued take-off, measured from liftoff, are shown against the runway 09 mast (Figure 6).

Appendix F: Timeline

  • 07:35:00 The aerodrome operator carried out the day's only movement area inspection, before the first scheduled arrival, with the result recorded as movement area clear. No further inspection was carried out or requested that day.
  • 17:16:00 The doors were closed, on schedule. This was the fifth sector of the crew's duty, the evening rotation having been added that morning when a member of the rostered crew reported unfit. Scheduled off blocks was 17:20, with 44 passengers, 2 flight crew and 1 cabin crew on board.
  • 17:21:50 The crew switched on the pilot-activated runway lighting.
  • 17:29:10 The crew broadcast their lining-up call on the CTAF for runway 09, because Tarlton Springs has no control tower. The wind from the AWIS was 090 at 6 kt. The crew requested no runway inspection and the aerodrome offered none, and no wildlife transmission appears on the CTAF in the preceding 90 minutes.
  • 17:30:02 to 17:30:29 (27 s) The take-off roll was under way, with power set and both engines at 98.4% and 98.5% torque. The first officer was pilot flying.
  • 17:30:29 V1 was called at 112 kt, calculated for 20,800 kg, flap 10, dry runway 09 and a 5 kt headwind component.
  • 17:30:31 The first officer sighted two kangaroos crossing from the northern side of the runway to the south, at an estimated range of around 200 m, and called them. The aircraft reached VR, 116 kt, in the same second, and no rotate call was made.
  • 17:30:32 The take-off was rejected at 118 kt, with the pilot in command taking control. Power levers reached flight idle within 0.6 seconds, 6 kt and 3 seconds past V1, with 695 m of sealed runway remaining.
  • 17:30:33 The aircraft struck both animals, with a lateral acceleration spike of 0.31 g right and a vertical spike of 1.48 g. Three No. 2 propeller blades were damaged beyond limits, its pitch change actuator was breached, and No. 2 reverse was unavailable for the rest of the stop. Remains and debris damaged the right inboard flap and the wing lower surface aft of the nacelle.
  • 17:30:34 to 17:30:51 (17 s) Maximum braking was established 2 seconds after the decision, against a fleet mean of 3.2 seconds, with anti-skid active on all four wheels. No. 1 reverse was selected at 17:30:36.
  • 17:30:51 The aircraft departed the sealed surface at 21 kt, and deceleration fell from 2.6 m/s2 on the seal to 1.9 m/s2 in graded gravel.
  • 17:30:57 The aircraft came to rest 62 m into the RESA, upright and on the extended centreline, with the nose wheel in graded gravel, 28 m short of the end of the prepared safety area. There was no fire.
  • 17:32:10 The aerodrome reporting officer activated the aerodrome emergency plan at the pilot in command's request on the CTAF. A vehicle was dispatched and the runway was broadcast as obstructed and the aerodrome closed. No injuries were reported at that stage and no assistance was requested.
  • 17:34:40 to 17:38:48 (4 m 08 s) Passengers disembarked by the forward airstair, with no evacuation commanded and no slides deployed. The main cabin lights were on throughout, and passengers were clear 4 minutes 8 seconds after the aircraft stopped.

Appendix G: Handling of sources

The pilot in command's air safety report ASR-2026-1184 was submitted under a confidential or just-culture reporting scheme. It may be attributed by role and must not be quoted verbatim, and identifying detail in it is not reproduced. The investigator's descriptions of recorded data, the sighting log, the works register, the inspection and structures reports, the performance assessment, the crew and duty records, the photometric check and the cabin lighting check are summarised in this report and are not quoted.
